subtype: Real hurt versus a habitual role [Observer]
passage: At the logistics firm's Thursday team meeting, Manoj again explained why the shipment delay wasn't his fault: the vendor had lied, IT had sabotaged him, and the manager "always had it in for him". Kiran had heard a version of this every month for a year; in each story Manoj was the one suffering and someone else was the villain. Then Tenzin spoke, voice sharp and shaking. Her client file had been deleted by someone else's login, and she had been blamed in an email to the whole team. She wasn't calm. She interrupted twice. A few colleagues rolled their eyes. "Another drama." Kiran almost did too, then remembered that Tenzin had never once complained in two years, and that a login record was something anyone could check. After the meeting Kiran walked over to Tenzin's desk. "Want help pulling the access log for the manager?" Tenzin's shoulders dropped. "Yes. Please."

qa.q: What did Tenzin say had happened to her client file?
qa.a: It had been deleted by someone else's login, and she had been blamed in an email to the whole team.

qa.q: What made Kiran hesitate before judging Tenzin?
qa.a: Kiran was tempted to dismiss her as dramatic, then felt doubtful of that reaction on remembering that Tenzin had never once complained in two years.

qa.q: How did Kiran avoid misjudging Tenzin?
qa.a: Kiran looked at her record and at facts anyone could check, like the access log, instead of her tone, and offered practical help.

qa.q: How might Tenzin have felt when colleagues rolled their eyes?
qa.a: Tenzin likely felt unheard and more upset, since being truly wronged and then dismissed as drama adds a second hurt.

grounding: Shows a colleague telling apart a person whose every story casts them as the sufferer from someone truly wronged who was not calm.

passage: Rain streaked the window of the café in Malmö while Anders talked for forty minutes. His boss was unfair, his ex had turned their friends against him, and now Emil, of all people, had "abandoned" him by not covering his weekend shifts at the bike shop. Emil listened, nodding, stirring a cold coffee. Anders was genuinely low; his eyes were puffy and his jacket hadn't been washed in a while. When Anders finally paused, Emil said, "That sounds like a rough month. I'm sorry. What do you want to do about the job?" Anders blinked. "I mean... if you'd just take Saturday..." "I can't do Saturdays, I told you that. I can help you write to your boss about the schedule tonight, if you want." Anders looked annoyed, then tired. "Fine. Tonight." Emil paid for both coffees and felt steadier than usual walking home.

qa.q: How long did Anders talk at the café?
qa.a: Anders talked for forty minutes.

qa.q: How did Emil feel walking home?
qa.a: Emil felt steadier than usual, having shown real care without giving up the limit on Saturdays.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Asking Anders what he wanted to do and offering to help write to his boss respected his pain while keeping Emil's limit on Saturday shifts.

qa.q: How did Anders take being refused?
qa.a: Anders looked annoyed, then tired, but agreed to write to his boss, which suggests part of him was ready to act.

grounding: Shows a person listening kindly, asking what the other wants to do, and staying firm about their own limits without accepting blame.

subtype: Threatening loss to get a yes [Actor]
passage: I'm Ishita, and this is the part of the story I don't love telling. Last year Vasudha, my best friend since school, got into a design course in Ahmedabad. I was staying in Indore. The night she told me, I said, "If you go, we're done. And I'll tell everyone what you told me about your parents." I'd never threatened anyone in my life. She cried, and said she'd think about not going. For a week I felt relieved, like I'd won. Then I saw her at the station, dropping her cousin, looking grey and scared, and she flinched when I waved. That's when I got it. I wasn't keeping a friend, I was holding one hostage. Underneath it was plain fear: everyone leaves me. I called her that night and said, "Go. I won't tell anyone anything. I'm sorry." I started seeing the college counsellor about that fear. She went. We talk on Sundays now.

qa.q: Where did Vasudha get into a design course?
qa.a: In Ahmedabad.

qa.q: What feeling was underneath Ishita's threat?
qa.a: Ishita felt a plain fear of abandonment, that everyone leaves, and even felt relieved for a week when Vasudha said she might not go.

qa.q: What did Ishita do to repair the harm?
qa.a: Ishita called that night, withdrew the threat, apologised, and began seeing the college counsellor about the fear behind it.

qa.q: How did the threat affect Vasudha?
qa.a: Vasudha cried, looked grey and scared, and flinched at a wave, showing the threat made her fearful rather than closer.

grounding: Shows a young adult threatening to end a friendship and expose a secret unless a friend gave in, driven by fear of abandonment, with coercion as the effect.

passage:
Tuesday night
Skipped Rakesh's birthday again. Third plan this month. Gautam said if I went, he'd finally tell my parents about the backlog paper and move out, and then who'd split the rent? When I said no to him last month, he didn't talk for days and then cried that I'm the only one he has.
And I believe him, that's the thing. I feel sorry for him. He really doesn't have many people. But I'm also scared every time my phone lights up.
I can't tell anymore which things I want and which things I do so he won't explode. Do I even still like badminton, or did I stop because he hated me going?
Tonight I called Anu-di and told her everything. She was quiet, then said, "This isn't your fault, and his threats aren't yours to fix. Let's go to your college counsellor together on Thursday." I feel lighter than I have in weeks.
Naveen

qa.q: Whose birthday did Naveen skip?
qa.a: Rakesh's birthday.

qa.q: What mix of feelings does Naveen have about Gautam?
qa.a: Naveen feels sorry for Gautam, who doesn't have many people, and scared every time the phone lights up, which blurs where Naveen's own choices end.

qa.q: Why was calling Anu-di a good step?
qa.a: Telling a trusted person broke the isolation; Anu-di said it wasn't Naveen's fault and planned a visit to the college counsellor together.

qa.q: How does Anu-di respond to what Naveen shares?
qa.a: Anu-di takes it seriously, says it isn't Naveen's fault and the threats aren't Naveen's to fix, and offers to go to the counsellor together.

grounding: Shows a young adult giving up friends and plans because saying no brings threats of exposure and loss, feeling both pity and fear.

subtype: Refusing the threat and getting support [Response]
passage:
Friday, 11:30 pm
Writing this now because my hands have only just stopped shaking.
At dinner I told Jomon I'm taking the Kochi job and moving out next month. He went very still, then said, "If you leave, I don't know what I'll do to myself."
Two years ago I'd have said, fine, I'll stay. Tonight I said, "I care about you a lot. I'm still taking the job. And I'm taking what you just said seriously." I didn't leave him alone. I sat with him on the sofa and called his sister Mercy; she came over within the hour. While we waited I rang a helpline, and they talked me through what to say and what to watch for. Mercy is staying the night, and she'll take him to see a doctor tomorrow.
I'm not guilty for having my own life. I'm also not walking away from him.
Thomas

qa.q: Who did Thomas call to come over?
qa.a: Jomon's sister Mercy.

qa.q: How was Thomas feeling while writing the entry?
qa.a: Thomas still felt shaken, with hands only just steady, but also clear and not guilty about having a life of Thomas's own.

qa.q: What made Thomas's response wise?
qa.a: Thomas stayed kind but did not give in, took the words seriously, stayed with Jomon, and brought in Mercy and a helpline the same night.

qa.q: How might Mercy see Thomas's call?
qa.a: Mercy likely felt worried but grateful to be told, since it let her be with her brother that night and take him to a doctor.

grounding: Shows a person who stays kind but refuses to give in to a threat, and involves family and a helpline the same night because safety is at risk.

passage: Sit, Pooja. You asked how you know if someone is controlling. Let me tell you about Sunita. We were twenty, in the same college in Nagpur, and she started seeing Mahesh from the hostel. First month, all sweetness. Then he began taking her phone at the canteen and scrolling through it. "I just worry about you," he'd say. He decided she shouldn't come to our study group because "those boys look at you". If she laughed with me, he went cold all evening. Everyone said, he's so caring. I thought so too, at first. What changed my mind was small: Sunita started asking him before ordering her own tea. So I asked her, alone, on the library steps, "Do you feel free with him?" She didn't answer. She just cried. We went to the college counsellor together that week. You know me as Lokesh mama, but back then I was only a worried friend, and that question is still the best one I know.

qa.q: What did Mahesh say when he took Sunita's phone?
qa.a: He said, “I just worry about you.”

qa.q: What was Lokesh feeling when Sunita started asking permission for her own tea?
qa.a: Lokesh felt worried and uneasy, because the small sign showed the so-called caring was taking away Sunita's freedom.

qa.q: Which choice in the story made a difference?
qa.a: Asking Sunita alone whether she felt free with Mahesh, then going with her to the college counsellor, gave her a safe way to face what was happening.

qa.q: How might Sunita have experienced Mahesh's attention at the start?
qa.a: At first it probably felt like love and care, which is why the control was hard to see until Lokesh's question made her cry.

grounding: Shows a young adult noticing a friend's partner checking her phone, choosing her friends and turning jealous, all described as care, and asking whether she feels free.

passage: You're getting married next year, so I'll tell you something I'm not proud of. I was twenty-five when Sudha and I married. I told myself I loved her more than anyone could. So I kept her salary card "safely" with me. I checked who called her. When she wore the yellow kurta to her friend's wedding, I said it was too much until she changed. I called all of it worry. Really, I was scared. If she had her own money, her own friends, her own opinions, maybe she wouldn't need me. So I made her world small enough to fit inside my rules. One evening her younger sister visited and said, in front of me, "Didi, you used to laugh so much." Sudha didn't answer. That silence hit me harder than any shout. The next week I handed back the card, and later I went to a counsellor, because I couldn't untangle the fear alone. Your Sumit chacha had to learn that love keeps no lock on anyone.

qa.q: What did Sumit keep “safely” with him?
qa.a: Sudha's salary card.

qa.q: What was really behind Sumit's worry?
qa.a: Sumit felt scared that if Sudha had her own money, friends and opinions she wouldn't need him, so fear of losing his hold drove the control.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and what did Sumit do after it?
qa.a: Sudha's sister saying she used to laugh so much, and Sudha's silence; Sumit then handed back the card and later went to a counsellor.

qa.q: What was life like for Sudha under these rules?
qa.a: Sudha's world shrank to fit Sumit's rules: her money, calls and clothes were checked, and she stopped laughing, going silent even when her sister noticed.

grounding: Shows a partner controlling money, calls, clothes and friends while calling it love, driven by fear of losing power, as the other's life shrinks.

subtype: A world that keeps getting smaller [Receiver]
passage:
January: Afreen missed Ritu's housewarming. Salman didn't like her going to places "full of strangers", and it was easier to say she had a headache. She told herself it was one party.
March: Afreen stood in the shop holding two dupattas and texted Salman photos of both before buying. She planned what to say before he came home and read his mood from the way he shut the door. When Ritu called, she answered from the balcony in a whisper. "He's never hit me," she said, when Ritu asked if she was okay. "He just worries."
May: Ritu came over at lunch with biryani and a printed page from a women's helpline. Afreen read the list: checking plans with a partner, seeing friends less, fearing their mood. She had lived almost all of it. "I didn't think it counted without bruises," she whispered. That afternoon, with Ritu beside her, she called the helpline, and a counsellor talked her through what could come next.

qa.q: What did Afreen text Salman from the shop?
qa.a: Photos of both dupattas before buying.

qa.q: How was Afreen feeling by March?
qa.a: Afreen felt anxious and on edge, planning what to say and reading Salman's mood from the way he shut the door.

qa.q: What did Ritu do that helped?
qa.a: Ritu stayed in touch, brought food and a helpline page without blame, and sat beside Afreen while she called the helpline.

qa.q: How might Ritu have felt hearing Afreen whisper from the balcony?
qa.a: Ritu likely felt worried and sad, sensing her friend's world shrinking, which is why she kept calling and later came with the page.

grounding: Shows a person gradually dropping friends, checking every choice and fearing a partner's mood, not calling it abuse because there are no bruises.

subtype: Signs a friend or family may notice [Observer]
passage: People ask what we noticed first, as Seema's family. Honestly, small things. My sister used to call Ammi every evening; then it became Sundays, then only when her husband was home, on speaker. At Eid she kept sending him photos: "I'm at Ammi's, see." She said she had no money for gifts, and Seema has earned her own salary since she was twenty-two. My first instinct was to storm over and say, "Pack your bags, you're coming home." Our aunt did exactly that, and Seema didn't speak to her for three months. So I, Irfan, the loud brother, learned to be quiet. I message her about silly things, cricket, recipes. I never say his name with anger. Once I told her, "Whatever happens, my door is open, no questions." Last week, for the first time, she asked if we could meet at the library, just the two of us.

qa.q: How did Seema's calls to Ammi change?
qa.a: From every evening to Sundays, then only when her husband was home, on speaker.

qa.q: What was Irfan's first instinct, and why did he hold back?
qa.a: Irfan felt angry and protective and wanted to storm over, but held back after seeing Seema stop speaking to their aunt for three months.

qa.q: What could Irfan do if Seema opens up at the library?
qa.a: Listen without blame, let Seema lead, and offer to help her reach a helpline or support service when she's ready, so any step is planned safely.

qa.q: Why might Seema have cut off the aunt who told her to pack her bags?
qa.a: Pressure to leave may have made Seema feel judged and cornered, pushing her away from the family and further into isolation.

grounding: Shows a relative noticing isolation, constant reporting of whereabouts and loss of her own money, and staying in touch without blame.

passage: In the kasba, Urmila waited until Hemant left for the mandi on Tuesday morning. Her hands shook as she walked to the anganwadi centre, where Kamla-didi, the worker she had known since childhood, was sorting ration slips. "Didi, I need to talk, but he mustn't find out yet." Kamla-didi shut the door and listened. She didn't say, just leave him. She said, "You're not to blame, and you're not alone. Let's call the women's helpline from my phone." The counsellor on the line spoke slowly: what was happening at home, who she trusted, whether her ID papers were somewhere safe. "Don't take any big step alone," the counsellor said. "Leaving can be the riskiest time. We'll plan it with you." Urmila walked home past the temple with the number memorised and a meeting with the protection officer on Friday. For the first time in months, the anger in her chest felt like strength, not fear.

qa.q: Where did Urmila go when Hemant left for the mandi?
qa.a: She walked to the anganwadi centre to see Kamla-didi.

qa.q: How did Urmila feel walking home past the temple?
qa.a: Urmila felt stronger; the anger in her chest felt like strength, not fear, and she trusted that she was not alone.

qa.q: Why did the counsellor advise against any big step alone?
qa.a: Because leaving can be the riskiest time, so planning with experts, such as the Friday meeting with the protection officer, keeps Urmila safer.

qa.q: How did Kamla-didi see her own role?
qa.a: Kamla-didi acted as a safe listener, not a judge: she shut the door, said Urmila wasn't to blame, and connected her to the helpline.

grounding: Shows a person quietly reaching a trusted person and a helpline, and planning for safety with experts before any big step.
